section_summary: This section follows U.S. efforts in 1935 to secure a convention restricting Japanese salmon packing in Bering Sea waters off Alaska. Embassy reports weigh Japanese crab and salmon operations against concurrent Soviet-Japanese fishery negotiations, while State and Commerce arrange an informal approach and technical assistance. In November, Japan declines negotiations for the time being, citing limited present activity and a desire to retain control over future fishing licenses. The section also includes correspondence on Japanese lobster shipments through Los Angeles and navigation rules for foreign fishing vessels.

subfiles.title: Japanese lobster fleet and transshipment through Los Angeles
subfiles.from: Alfred A. Cohn, Collector of Customs, Los Angeles
subfiles.about: Cohn reports a proposed Japanese fleet fishing Mexican lobster concessions and routing the catch through Los Angeles.
subfiles.summary: Cohn sees no apparent legal bar if regulations are followed, but urges Navy and State scrutiny.

subfiles.title: Customs response on Japanese lobster transshipment
subfiles.about: Customs finds no objection under its regulations to transshipping fish from Japanese vessels at Los Angeles.
subfiles.summary: The commissioner identifies the immediate-exportation procedure and refers the matter to Navy, State, and navigation officials.

subfiles.title: Radio equipment on Japanese fishing vessels
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Navy concerns about long-range radio aboard Japanese vessels fishing off the Pacific Coast.
subfiles.summary: A State Department officer has referred the concern to an interdepartmental fisheries committee.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for file enclosure
subfiles.about: A file charge slip records handling of an enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Administrative charge slip with file numbers and initials.

subfiles.title: Telegram on timing of fishery approach
subfiles.about: The embassy says its mailed report recommends delay pending Russo-Japanese fishery discussions.
subfiles.summary: The report has been mailed; it suggests postponing an American approach.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1190 on northern fisheries
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew assesses Japanese fishing off Alaska and recommends delaying a formal approach until Soviet-Japanese negotiations advance.
subfiles.summary: Japanese vessels are expected to expand crab and fish-meal operations near Alaska, but the embassy finds no immediate plan to pack salmon there. Grew describes Japanese deep-sea salmon fishing, a proposed control law, and difficult negotiations with the Soviet Union. He favors a later informal inquiry about American wishes, perhaps in late summer or early autumn.

subfiles.title: Neville-Kurusu conversation on fisheries
subfiles.about: Kurusu discusses Japanese crab fishing near Alaska and shares Fisheries Bureau information.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu expects Bering Sea fishing to continue and supplies a note on planned vessels.

subfiles.title: Translated statement by Fisheries Bureau official Ide
subfiles.about: Ide describes crab and fish-meal vessels and the reach of a proposed deep-sea fishery law.
subfiles.summary: The statement projects three crab vessels and a fish-meal vessel east of 180 degrees longitude in 1935. It says their gear will not take salmon. The proposed law is aimed principally at fishing near Soviet territory but could extend farther east.

subfiles.title: New measures for North Sea fishing
subfiles.doc_type: enclosure; translated press article and draft law
subfiles.about: A translated article explains Japan’s proposed law controlling northern fishing companies.
subfiles.summary: The article links the bill to consolidation of Japanese fishing interests, protection of the Nichiro company, and anticipated revision of the Soviet-Japanese convention. The draft gives the competent minister broad authority over company management, financing, fishing rights, reporting, and sanctions. It also sets penalties for unauthorized fishing.

subfiles.title: State Department letter forwarding Grew’s despatch
subfiles.from: William Phillips, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: State forwards Grew’s advice to postpone approaching Japan on a salmon-fishing treaty.
subfiles.summary: Grew recommends waiting for Japanese legislation and progress in Soviet-Japanese fishery negotiations.

subfiles.title: Document file note for Telegram No. 68
subfiles.about: A file note indexes the attached Tokyo telegram on foreign exploitation of Japanese natural resources.
subfiles.summary: Indexes Telegram No. 68 and its discussion of commercial fishing licenses.

subfiles.title: Japanese rules and policies affecting foreign resource exploitation
subfiles.about: Grew describes legal and administrative barriers to foreign fishing and other enterprises in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Although no express law bars foreign commercial fishing, licenses for foreign interests are unlikely. The telegram also discusses water power, agriculture, subsidies, and immigration.

subfiles.title: Commerce urges prompt salmon treaty
subfiles.about: Commerce urges treaty negotiations as soon as diplomatic conditions permit.
subfiles.summary: Commerce accepts Grew’s judgment on timing but warns that improved Japanese deep-sea techniques could threaten Alaskan salmon runs and American investment.

subfiles.title: State response to Commerce on treaty timing
subfiles.from: William Phillips, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: State agrees on urgency and directs the embassy to watch for a favorable approach to Japan.
subfiles.summary: State says enactment of Japan’s fishery bill need not be awaited and forwards news that the bill failed.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 748 on approaching Japan
subfiles.from: William Phillips, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: State instructs Grew to assess when an informal Japanese approach on salmon conservation would be timely.
subfiles.summary: The instruction favors an informal inquiry after Soviet-Japanese negotiations have had a reasonable opportunity to progress. It rejects waiting for enactment of Japan’s proposed fishing law and asks the embassy to report when an approach seems opportune.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note on Japanese fishing licenses
subfiles.about: The note argues that existing Japanese licensing powers could enforce a fishery convention.
subfiles.summary: Failure of the northern fisheries bill need not prevent Japan from controlling vessels off Alaska.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1228 on failed northern fisheries bill
subfiles.about: Grew reports that Japan’s proposed northern fisheries control law failed in the Diet.
subfiles.summary: The House of Peers passed the bill, but the lower house did not act before adjournment. Grew relates its failure to preparations for revising the Soviet-Japanese convention and to divisions among Japanese fishing interests.

subfiles.title: Telephone note on Commerce’s understanding
subfiles.about: A State officer confirms with Dr. Bowers that Commerce understands State’s preferred treaty timing.
subfiles.summary: Commerce agrees that Japan’s pending law need not delay an approach; its May 7 letter needs no reply.

subfiles.title: Commerce letter on continuing threat to Alaskan salmon
subfiles.about: Commerce reiterates concern that Japanese fishery disputes may redirect vessels toward Alaska.
subfiles.summary: It welcomes a treaty barring Japanese fishing in specified Bering Sea and Bristol Bay waters.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1298 requesting precise negotiating instructions
subfiles.about: Grew requests clarity on species and waters before talks and recommends a fisheries expert.
subfiles.summary: The embassy will report when an informal approach seems timely. Grew cautions that adding demands after talks begin could require concessions and suggests sending a Bureau of Fisheries specialist.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 118 proposing tentative approach
subfiles.about: Grew asks authority for a tentative informal discussion with Japan despite protracted Soviet-Japanese talks.
subfiles.summary: An approach would signal American concern and help the embassy judge Japan’s position.

subfiles.title: State asks Commerce how to answer Grew
subfiles.about: State seeks Commerce’s views on Grew’s proposed informal approach to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter forwards Grew’s request for precise instructions and reports his suggestion that Japan be told promptly of American concern.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1318 on Japanese-Soviet fishery talks
subfiles.about: Grew reports that Japanese officials remain occupied with Soviet fishery negotiations.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese seek changes to fishery-lot auctions, while denunciation of the existing convention has opened broader talks. Grew advises waiting for an easing of tension before approaching Japan.

subfiles.title: Neville-Togo conversation on Bering Sea fisheries
subfiles.about: Togo discusses Japanese crab vessels and the timing of any U.S.-Japanese fishery talks.
subfiles.summary: Togo says the vessels are not equipped for salmon and should stay roughly twenty miles offshore. He acknowledges American concern but says officials are occupied with unsettled Kamchatka fisheries.

subfiles.title: State forwards Despatch No. 1318 and requests expert assistance
subfiles.from: William Phillips, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: State asks Commerce to prepare technical assistance for eventual fishery talks in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The letter notes the embassy’s May 21 report of Japanese preoccupation, while emphasizing Grew’s later June 3 suggestion to approach Japan. Expert help would reduce delays during negotiations.

subfiles.title: Routing note to the Secretary
subfiles.about: A division officer forwards a requested memorandum on the fishery question.
subfiles.summary: Notes earlier discussion with the Under Secretary by Mr. Dooman.

subfiles.title: Handwritten file note
subfiles.about: A brief handwritten note appears to refer to Secretary Roper.
subfiles.summary: The remaining text is illegible in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Reasons to secure fisheries expertise for Tokyo
subfiles.about: The division explains why technical assistance should be arranged before substantive treaty talks.
subfiles.summary: Earlier embassy correspondence repeatedly identifies a need for expert support. The memorandum cites Dooman’s view that Tokyo should defer action if Commerce cannot send an expert, recalls Ambassador Forbes’s similar 1931 request, and argues for a formal agreement before Japanese investment off Alaska grows.

subfiles.title: State’s formal request for a fisheries expert
subfiles.about: State asks Commerce to confirm it can provide technical help for talks in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The letter explains that expert advice would keep negotiations moving and avoid repeated referrals to Washington. It says final authority to begin talks is being withheld pending Commerce’s answer. State also cites the risk that informal Japanese restraint may not last and favors an agreement before substantial Japanese investment develops.

subfiles.title: Commerce approves approach and offers Ward T. Bower
subfiles.about: Commerce supports an informal Japanese approach focused on salmon and offers Bower’s services.
subfiles.summary: Commerce limits the U.S. objective to salmon preservation, suggests possible flexibility on Japanese crab fishing, and offers Ward T. Bower when expert assistance is needed.

subfiles.title: Instruction authorizing informal inquiry in Tokyo
subfiles.about: State authorizes an informal inquiry about a convention barring Japanese salmon packing in specified Bering Sea waters.
subfiles.summary: The embassy may discuss sympathetic consideration of Japanese crab proposals. It is to keep initial discussions limited, call for Ward T. Bower when Japan shows active interest, and consult earlier instructions before approaching the Foreign Office.

subfiles.title: State reports instructions to Tokyo
subfiles.about: Hull informs Commerce that Tokyo has been instructed to open cautious informal discussions.
subfiles.summary: The embassy will await clear Japanese interest before requesting a fisheries expert.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 163 reporting first Japanese approach
subfiles.about: Neville reports his informal inquiry to Vice Minister Shigemitsu about a salmon-packing convention.
subfiles.summary: Neville supplies a written formulation covering the Cape Avinof–Cape Sarichef line and possible crab-fishing proposals. Shigemitsu promises to consult the responsible department and asks whether the United States would then submit formal proposals.

subfiles.title: State forwards Neville’s report to Commerce
subfiles.about: State forwards the chargé’s report of his August 7 discussion with Japan’s vice minister.
subfiles.summary: The letter encloses the Tokyo telegram for Commerce’s information.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1425 on Japanese response and next steps
subfiles.about: Neville assesses his conversation with the vice minister and recommends preparing proposals and an expert.
subfiles.summary: Neville expects a possibly favorable Japanese reply. If one arrives, he recommends that Bower bring a draft convention to Tokyo and that substantive talks pause until his arrival. He encloses an earlier conversation with F. S. Booth about Japanese offshore fishing.

subfiles.title: Neville-Booth conversation on Japanese offshore fisheries
subfiles.about: Booth describes Japanese salmon methods, floating canneries, and crab operations.
subfiles.summary: Booth distinguishes boats based in the Kuriles from floating salmon canneries off Kamchatka. He expects Nichiro to let costly floating canneries decline after Soviet negotiations. He considers Bering Sea crab fishing marginal and Japanese salmon packing off Alaska unlikely under current conditions.

subfiles.title: Instruction on formal proposals and Bower’s travel
subfiles.about: State tells Tokyo it can promise specific proposals and arrange Bower’s immediate travel after an affirmative reply.
subfiles.summary: No draft convention exists yet; Bower will carry instructions on possible inducements.

subfiles.title: Navigation-law answers on foreign fishing vessels
subfiles.about: Weaver answers whether fishing vessels may enter U.S. ports from, or clear for, the high seas.
subfiles.summary: A properly cleared foreign vessel may enter and land high-seas fish subject to customs requirements. U.S. law provides no clearance to or entry from the high seas as a destination, but does not bar an American vessel from carrying a floating plant’s output ashore.

subfiles.title: Bureau of Fisheries inquiry on Japanese crab canneries
subfiles.about: The bureau asks whether Japanese floating crab canneries can land catch directly in U.S. ports and obtain clearance.
subfiles.summary: The inquiry also asks about transfer to American vessels. It considers direct landing, tariff reduction, and supplies from U.S. ports as possible inducements for a salmon-fishing treaty.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 208: Japan declines negotiations
subfiles.about: Neville reports Japan’s refusal to negotiate a salmon and crab convention at present.
subfiles.summary: Japanese officials say current Bristol Bay interests are small, open-sea salmon licenses are confined to Kamchatka, and no treaty is immediately needed. They also wish to retain discretion over a large area. Neville stresses American investment and asks for instructions, suggesting Japan might offer a counterproposal if pressed.

subfiles.title: State seeks Commerce’s response to Japanese refusal
subfiles.about: Hull forwards Neville’s report and asks Commerce what instructions should follow.
subfiles.summary: The letter highlights Neville’s thought that continued pressure might elicit a Japanese counterproposal.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Telegram No. 208
subfiles.about: The paraphrase begins to restate Japan’s reasons for declining fishery negotiations.
subfiles.summary: Japan cites limited current fishing activity and its wish to retain freedom of action in the proposed area.
